problem:
A body of mass $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons $(\text{N}).$  At time $t>0$ seconds, the position of the body is given by $s(t)={e}^{2t}$ meters.

Calculate the magnitude of the force at time $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}$ seconds. Do not round the answer.

The magnitude of the force equals
{{field-1}} $\text{N}.$
worked_solution:
According to Newton’s second law,

$$
F(t)=ma(t),
$$

 
where $F(t)$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a(t)$ is the acceleration.

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t}) \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{2t}) \\  & =2\cdot 2{e}^{2t} \\  & =4{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the acceleration at $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}\,\text{s}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}) & =4{e}^{2\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}} \\  & =4{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}]} \\  & =4{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =4\cdot 2 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force in Newtons is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}) & =ma(\operatorname{ln}⁡\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 8 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of the force is

$$
|F(2)|=|2|=2\,\text{N}.
$$
